Commenter on the security exploit: while the exploit ran, CodeRabbit still reviewed the malicious PR and posted a comment flagging a critical security risk, yet the application executed the attacker's code anyway because it didn't realize it was running on its own production system.
User praise: "I've noticed CodeRabbit at times does reviews that are super. It is able to catch bugs that even claude code misses on our Github PRs. Blows my mind at times tbh."
Team that removed CodeRabbit: "We removed it as it was mostly too verbose, catching too many false positives and never really added anything useful."
Reply on verbosity and false positives: you can comment on this in the PR and supposedly CodeRabbit will remember and get better over time.
Skeptical reply to the claim that CodeRabbit catches bugs Claude Code misses: "Is that good? I assume it just catches a different 10% of the bugs."

Paid user cancelled their CodeRabbit subscription, saying it worried them that a post had to go viral on HN before the company acknowledged the vulnerability. They noted CodeRabbit's blog had no mention of it, and that lack of transparency makes the company look bad.

Criticism of the breach: CodeRabbit's GitHub App private key was sitting in environment variables, accessible to the Rubocop linter that ran untrusted repo code. GitHub's own docs warn against storing it there; commenters called it basic secrets mismanagement and "amateur level of security."

Users questioned why CodeRabbit needs write access to repos at all. Others explained it can write tests and offer directly committable fixes. Critics said a third-party review app holding write permission across ~1M repos is a dangerous design.

Suggested workaround for the write-access concern: use a GitHub Action triggered on pull_request_target that calls CodeRabbit's API to generate a patch and pushes it, or have CodeRabbit just propose suggested changes, rather than granting the app broad write power.
Positive note on the incident response: "Props to the CodeRabbit team" for responding and remediating quickly, in contrast to other vendors the researchers contacted, who never responded.

Commenter said the first time they saw CodeRabbit was a Twitter ad containing a "comically" bad code suggestion, and that they can't take the company seriously given that was supposedly its best showcase.

Skepticism of the CEO's explanation that only Rubocop ran outside the sandbox: "Honestly, that last part sounds like a lie. Why would one task run in a drastically different architectural situation, and it happen to be the one exploited?"

Open-source maintainer: enabled CodeRabbit on a few repos and the experience is "pretty good, it's better than expected, best of the limited number of code review tools I have experience with." Having an extra active AI "maintainer" adds confidence.
User comment: "Love the product clean, actionable PR reviews."

User of several AI review tools has mixed feelings: productized AI review carries a conflict of interest when you can't control the models or prompts, causing pain for a mission-critical process. They also suspect most of CodeRabbit's $10M OSS pledge is product credit rather than cash donations.
Reaction to CodeRabbit's OSS milestone post: "Is this the app that exposed their read/write github keys to a million repos?", showing the security incident still shapes perception.
